title: The Mountain That Ate Men: Potosí and the Silver of the World

intro: In April 1545 Spanish miners at Porco, in the high Andes of what was then called Upper Peru, registered claims on a red cone of a mountain some 4,000 metres up, in a cold, treeless puna where nothing grew but a little grass. Within a few years the camp at its foot, Potosí, was one of the largest towns in the Americas, and the Cerro Rico, the Rich Hill, was the single greatest source of silver in the world. Its silver paid for Spanish armies in Europe, passed through Seville into the money of Genoa, Antwerp and beyond, and crossed the Pacific on the Manila galleons after 1571 to be traded for Chinese silks and porcelain. The finder of the mountain is usually named as an Andean man, Diego Huallpa (Acosta in 1590 calls him Gualpa, of the Chumbivilcas people near Cuzco), who is said to have caught hold of a bush while chasing deer and seen rich ore in its roots. The story reaches the page only through Spanish chroniclers writing decades later, and it was embroidered further in the eighteenth century. No surviving firsthand account by Huallpa, or by any of the Andean men who first worked the veins, has been found. The honest record of Potosí in the sixteenth century is not a set of diaries. It is letters to the Council of the Indies and to Philip II, chronicles, a mine owner's report, a friar's memorial, the petitions of Andean lords, treasury registers summarised by chroniclers, and, later, the drawings of an Andean author. They are set here with their forms named plainly. Some of the most vivid voices, such as Guaman Poma de Ayala (c. 1615) and Bartolomé Arzáns de Orsúa y Vela (1700s), wrote after 1600 and are labelled as later or secondhand for these years. Two technical and political changes turned a boom of the 1540s and 1550s into a system that lasted two and a half centuries. In the early 1570s the mercury amalgamation process, already used in New Spain, was brought to Potosí, using mercury from Huancavelica in central Peru; it made the lower-grade ores of the mountain profitable again. And Viceroy Francisco de Toledo organised the mita: a compulsory annual draft of Andean men aged about 18 to 50 from sixteen highland provinces, who were sent to Potosí to work in the mines and mills for low fixed wages. Figures for the size of the draft are given in this chapter as positions: about 13,500 a year in many accounts, 14,181 in the general allotment of 1578 as cited by one modern study, and 'over 11,000' in another reference work, with roughly a third working at any one time. How many people died because of the mines is not known. Contemporaries described men crushed in falls, broken by carrying ore up hide ladders in the dark, and sickened by cold and by mercury; one friar wrote in 1586 that half of twenty healthy men going in on Monday might come out crippled by Sunday. title: The Metals Hidden in the Ashes
eyes: Institut de France (First Class) and Napoleon Bonaparte
places: Brother and family biographer, writing in 1836
Como, writing to London; later Paris (1801) and Milan (1814)
Laboratory of the Royal Institution, Albemarle Street, London
London, writing in 1831 from Davy's papers and the Royal Institution's records
Royal Institution; then France and Italy with Davy, 1813–1815
École polytechnique and the Arcueil circle, Paris
intro: On 20 March 1800 Alessandro Volta, a professor at Pavia writing from Como, sent Sir Joseph Banks a long letter in French describing a stack of paired metal discs and brine-soaked card that gave a steady electric current. Before the Royal Society heard the letter on 26 June, two Londoners who had seen it, the surgeon Anthony Carlisle and the journal editor William Nicholson, built their own pile. They watched bubbles of gas rise from a wire dipped in a tube of water. Within a few weeks chemistry had a new tool that could pull compounds apart. Seven years later, in the basement laboratory of the Royal Institution in Albemarle Street, Humphry Davy turned the largest batteries he could gather on moistened potash. Small globules of a metal that looked like quicksilver broke through the crust. Some caught fire as they formed. Soda gave up a second metal a few days later. Davy called them potassium and sodium and announced them in the Bakerian Lecture of 19 November 1807. He then fell seriously ill for weeks. In 1808, helped by a method sent from Stockholm by Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Magnus Pontin, he took barium, strontium, calcium and magnesium (which he first called 'magnium') from the alkaline earths. In June of the same year he reached boron at almost the same moment as Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard in Paris. The record here is mostly papers, laboratory notes, institutional minutes and letters, not diaries, and the form tags say so. The famous scene of the discovery, Davy dancing about the room, comes from his cousin and assistant Edmund Davy, but only as his brother John Davy printed it in 1836, almost thirty years later. The laboratory register itself was read differently by Davy's first biographer, John Ayrton Paris, who in 1831 dated the great result to 19 October, not 6 October. Both readings are given here as positions. Two priority contests run through the chapter. In Paris, Gay-Lussac and Thénard made potassium in quantity by chemistry alone, heating potash with iron. They argued that Davy's metal might be a compound containing hydrogen, and they announced the decomposition of boracic acid nine days before Davy read his own, more tentative account. The other contest is a strange one: Napoleon's Institut awarded Davy its galvanism prize while Britain and France were at war. Davy is reported to have said that the countries might be at war but the men of science were not, while English newspapers argued he should refuse it. The chapter closes with a journey. In October 1813 Davy, newly married to Jane Apreece, crossed to France with a passport from the enemy government. With him went a young assistant, Michael Faraday, who kept a journal. In Paris Davy worked on the new substance later named iodine, and the Institut elected him a corresponding member. In June 1814 Faraday met Volta in person, and so the chapter ends with the man who began it.

title: The Mountain of Light Changes Hands

intro: On 29 March 1849, at the end of the Second Anglo-Sikh War, the ten-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh signed the terms that ended his kingdom. The Treaty of Lahore annexed the Punjab to British India. Its third article dealt with a single object: the gem called the Koh-i-Noor, which Maharaja Ranjit Singh had taken from Shah Shuja, was to be surrendered by the Maharaja of Lahore to the Queen of England. Lord Dalhousie, the Governor-General, insisted that the stone go to the Crown and not to the East India Company. The directors in London objected, and his letters home show him defending the choice for months. The stone already had a long history of seizure, and much of it is disputed. The diamond Babur describes in his memoirs has been identified with the Koh-i-Noor by some writers and denied by others; Valentine Ball and Nevil Story-Maskelyne argued the point in Nature in 1891. Nadir Shah carried it from Delhi to Persia after sacking the city in 1739. It passed to the Durrani rulers of Afghanistan and then to Shah Shuja. On 1 June 1813, by the account in the Lahore court chronicle of Sohan Lal Suri, Shah Shuja surrendered it to Ranjit Singh at Lahore. Ranjit wore it in an armlet at court. The sources for that phase include Persian chronicles, the recollections of the Kashmiri munshi Mohan Lal and stories told of Ranjit's minister Fakir Azizuddin. They are context here, not entries. This chapter follows the stone over three years. It went from the Lahore treasury, where the Scottish surgeon John Login kept the Toshakhana, to Dalhousie's own body: he carried it to Bombay sewn into a belt. From Bombay HMS Medea took it to England in 1850, with cholera aboard, a hostile reception at Mauritius and a storm on the way. It was presented to Queen Victoria on 3 July 1850, in the East India Company's 250th anniversary year. At the Great Exhibition of 1851 crowds found it a disappointment. In July 1852 it was recut in a London workshop, the Duke of Wellington making the first cut. The honest record is mostly letters, official minutes and receipts, newspapers, scientific papers and one later memoir; only Queen Victoria and Henry Cole kept diaries that touch it. The form tags say so. The people whose stone it was are the hardest to hear. No firsthand Sikh court account of the handover in 1849 was found for this chapter. Duleep Singh's own words survive only from later years: through Lady Login's memoir of 1890, which recalls him handing the recut stone back to the Queen in 1854, and through his letters of the 1880s, which call the annexation an injustice. Two well-known stories are later traditions. One is that John Lawrence left the diamond in a waistcoat pocket and his bearer found it in a tin box. The other is the 'curse' said to fall on any man who wears it. The anecdote is labelled as such in its entry. The curse is a legend, recorded by the Royal Collection as the reason only queens have worn the stone. A coda records positions, not verdicts. Duleep Singh pr

intro: On a Monday in January 1848 a Mormon labourer on a half-built sawmill in the Sierra foothills wrote one line in his diary: some kind of metal had turned up in the tail race, and it looked like gold. Within a year the President of the United States had confirmed the find to Congress. Within two, a hundred thousand newcomers were in California, the territory had become a state, and the people whose land it was were being killed, indentured and starved off it. This chapter sets the find and the rush side by side through people who stood in very different places. On the mill crew are Henry Bigler and Azariah Smith, wage hands who wanted only enough money to rejoin their families. The owner is John Sutter, whose fort and Native workforce dissolved in months. Then come the San Francisco weeklies that first shrugged and then folded; Walter Colton, magistrate of an emptying capital; Colonel Mason, who rode out to count; and President Polk, who made it official. The rush was never only an American story. Antonio Franco Coronel, a Californio from Los Angeles, and Vicente Pérez Rosales, a Chilean, struck gold early and were driven off their claims as 'foreigners' in 1849. Norman Asing, a Chinese merchant and naturalized citizen, answered the governor in print when the state turned on Chinese miners in 1852. Louise Clappe ('Dame Shirley') saw a camp riot against Spanish speakers and the whippings that followed. William Swain stands for the overland forty-niners who arrived when the easy gold was gone. Native Californians did much of the early digging: Mason counted them as more than half the miners in 1848, many working for white employers for goods. No firsthand written account by a Native Californian of these years has been found for this chapter. The Pomo record is William Ralganal Benson's narrative, published in 1932 from the testimony of men who took part. It is set beside the official record of Governor Peter Burnett: the statutes of 1850 and his 1851 message expecting a 'war of extermination'. Both are given plainly. The record is mixed, and the form tags say so. There are true diaries (Bigler, Smith, Colton's published diary, Pérez Rosales), dated letters (Clappe, Swain), newspapers, official reports and statutes, and recollections set down decades later (Sutter's 1857 article, Coronel's 1877 dictation, Benson's 1932 narrative). James Marshall's own later account and Mariano Vallejo's 1875 recollections are not used here. Disputed or legendary moments, such as Brannan's street cry, are marked as such.

title: The Rock on Which the Future Would Be Built
eyes: The diggings press: Diamond News, Diamond Field and Diggers' Gazette
Pedi, Sotho, Tsonga and other African migrant workers
places: Cape Town; visited the fields 1871 and 1872
Colesberg Kopje on the farm Vooruitzigt
Klipdrift and Pniel, then Dutoitspan and New Rush
London; visited the Hopetown district in 1868
Natal, then Dutoitspan and New Rush
The diggings and the roads to them
intro: In early 1867 a stone picked up by a child on a farm near Hopetown, on the Orange River, travelled by trader's pocket and post envelope to Grahamstown, where a doctor named William Atherstone pronounced it a diamond. Two years later a Griqua shepherd's find, the 83.5-carat Star of South Africa, changed hands for livestock and then for £11,200. By 1870 thousands of diggers were washing gravel on the Vaal at Klipdrift; by July 1871 a cook named Damon had sunk the shaft on a low hill at Vooruitzigt that became the New Rush, then Kimberley, then the deepest hand-dug hole in the world. The land was claimed by four powers at once. The Griqua under Nicolaas Waterboer held it by treaty and occupation; the Orange Free State had granted the farms on which the dry diggings lay; the South African Republic claimed the north bank of the Vaal; and Tswana chiefs, whose people had lived there longest, were barely heard. Britain resolved the dispute in its own favour: an arbitration award by Robert Keate on 17 October 1871 accepted the Griqua case, and ten days later Sir Henry Barkly proclaimed British sovereignty in Waterboer's name. The Griqua kept almost none of the land. The diggings became an experiment in controlling labour. White claimholders, organised in diggers' committees and speaking through the camp newspapers, demanded wage cuts, searches, curfews and an end to Black claimholding. In 1872 they burned tents, flogged suspected thieves and won registration rules and a pass law. Meanwhile more than 50,000 African men a year walked to the fields from Pedi, Sotho, Tsonga, Zulu and Tswana country, many to buy guns sold openly in Kimberley. In 1875 the diggers turned on the government itself in the Black Flag rising. Almost none of this record is diary. It is letters, official papers, an arbitration map, parliamentary answers, newspaper extracts and a few published journals by British visitors. The men who dug the hole left no writing of their own that has been found; their words survive only as complaints and affidavits taken down by officials, and through the reports of Gwayi Tyamzashe, an African minister who came to the fields in 1872. The eyes here are arranged so that the official claim, the diggers' paper and the workers' record can be read against each other on the same days.

title: The Table and Its Rivals
eyes: Royal Society of London (Council and medal records)
places: Away from the meeting (St Petersburg or the provinces)
Cognac (Charente); Wurtz's laboratory in Paris, autumn 1875
Royal Institution, London (read in his absence)
Russian Chemical Society, St Petersburg University
St Petersburg (note to the Paris Academy)
intro: On a winter morning in St Petersburg in 1869 (17 February by the Russian calendar, 1 March in the West) a chemistry professor cancelled a trip to inspect cheese cooperatives and spent the day shuffling the elements. By evening Dmitri Mendeleev had a printed sheet on its way to chemists across Europe, with blank spaces for elements nobody had seen. Seventeen days later his colleague Nikolai Menshutkin read it to the young Russian Chemical Society while its author was absent. This chapter is a priority ledger more than a diary. Its records are papers, letters to journals, a lithographed book, a printed sheet, society minutes, assay figures and medal citations, and the form tags say so. Laid side by side, they show that the idea of ordering elements by atomic weight was in the air for seven years. Chancourtois's helix appeared in Paris in 1862 with its diagram left out. Newlands's octaves were printed in a London trade weekly in 1864–65 and laughed at in the Chemical Society in 1866. Odling and Meyer printed tables in 1864, Hinrichs a spiral in Iowa in 1867, and Meyer his atomic-volume curve in 1870. What separated Mendeleev's system was not the order but the gaps. In 1871 he described three missing elements with figures: atomic weights, densities and oxides. Then the assayers and spectroscopists found them: Lecoq de Boisbaudran's gallium in 1875 in a Pyrenean zinc ore, Nilson's scandium in 1879 in Scandinavian rare earths, and Winkler's germanium in 1886, in a Saxon silver ore whose analysis came up seven per cent short. Each finder had his own relationship to the forecast. Lecoq resented being corrected on his density by a man who had never seen the metal, and found Mendeleev right. Winkler wrote to St Petersburg within three weeks. The positions are set out with their evidence and no verdict. The Royal Society's medals were the nearest thing the period had to rulings: Mendeleev and Meyer jointly in 1882, Newlands in 1887. Mendeleev's own famous story, the table seen in a dream, survives only as a colleague's later anecdote and is shown as legend beside the crossed-out drafts of the same day. The ores themselves were raised by miners at Pierrefitte and at the Himmelsfürst mine near Freiberg. No surviving firsthand account by them was found.

title: The Reef Under the Ridge
eyes: The Eastern Star / The Star (Thomas and George Sheffield, proprietors)
Hermann Eckstein (president), for the Witwatersrand Chamber of Mines
places: Coach from Kimberley to the Rand
Langlaagte farm, then Pretoria; vanished from the record late 1886
Main Reef properties, including the Ferreira
Wilgespruit farm, north of present Roodepoort
intro: In February 1886 two itinerant workmen building cottages on the farm Langlaagte, on the long quartzite ridge the Boers called the Witwatersrand, picked up a piece of conglomerate rock and crushed and panned it. What they found was not a vein but the outcrop of a reef that ran for miles and went down for thousands of feet: the richest goldfield ever found. Within seven months President Paul Kruger's South African Republic (ZAR) had proclaimed public diggings; within ten, a triangle of leftover government land called Randjeslaagte had been surveyed into stands and auctioned as Johannesburg. The record here is mostly not diaries. It is affidavits sworn by prospectors, government proclamations and departmental letters, company letters, newspaper files, Chamber of Mines reports, and memoirs written much later by men who were there. The question of who found the reef first was argued for fifty-five years: George Harrison made sworn statements in 1886 and was granted the discoverer's claim, while George Walker and George Honeyball told different stories decades afterwards. Those are set out here as positions, with their dates, and no verdict. The money came fast. J. B. Robinson arrived in July 1886 with a cheque from Alfred Beit; Cecil Rhodes and Charles Rudd bought more cautiously and founded the Gold Fields of South Africa in London in February 1887; Hermann Eckstein's firm at the Corner House became the centre of the Wernher-Beit interest. Then, in 1889, the oxidised ore near the surface gave way at depth to pyritic 'blue' rock from which mercury amalgamation recovered too little gold, and the share boom collapsed. The MacArthur-Forrest cyanide process, tried at the Salisbury mine in mid-1890, rescued the field and opened the way to deep-level mining. The men who did the digging were overwhelmingly African migrants, many from Portuguese Mozambique, working on contracts, under pass regulations and the Master and Servant law, for wages the mine owners combined to push down. The Chamber of Mines, founded in 1887 and reconstituted in 1889, recorded them as a labour supply. No surviving firsthand account by an African mineworker on the Rand for 1886–1891 has been found for this chapter; what they earned, where they came from and how they were controlled is known from the owners' own reports, and those reports are used here plainly for what they show. The same holds for the Indian traders whom the ZAR's Law 3 of 1885 barred from burgher rights and from owning land outside assigned locations, and for the Chinese storekeepers of early Johannesburg: their petitions survive in collections such as Bhana and Pachai's Documentary History, but no diary of theirs is used here. Between the burghers of the old republic and the uitlanders, the foreigners who outnumbered them in the new town, lay the quarrel that ran on to the Jameson Raid of December 1895. title: The Last Place of Decimals
places: London, theatre of the University of London, Burlington Gardens
Terling Place, Essex (letter printed in Nature, London)
Terling Place, Essex; London (Royal Institution, Royal Society)
his private laboratory, Notting Hill, London
intro: In 1892 the most careful weigher of gases in Britain admitted in print that he was puzzled. Nitrogen taken from the air was heavier, by about one part in a thousand, than nitrogen made from chemicals. Lord Rayleigh asked Nature's readers for help. Two years later the difference had a name, argon, and within six years five new elements had been added to a column of the periodic table that nobody had drawn. This is a laboratory chapter, and its record is mostly letters, papers, lectures and a few labelled objects rather than diaries. The closest thing to a daybook is Morris Travers's laboratory notebooks of 1898, which he turned into a book in 1928; the rest is a correspondence between a physicist in Essex and a chemist in Gower Street, the minutes of learned societies, and the weekly columns of Nature. One document was not read by anyone for 110 years: a sealed note Ramsay lodged in Paris in 1894. The eyes span a century. Henry Cavendish's bubble of 1785 is the first sighting; Janssen in India and Lockyer in Hampstead saw helium's yellow line in the sun in 1868; Rayleigh and Ramsay worked out argon in 1894–95; Crookes checked the spectra; Cleve and his student Langlet in Uppsala confirmed and weighed helium; Mendeleev in St Petersburg and Dewar across the corridor at the Royal Institution doubted that argon was an element at all, and suggested it was a dense nitrogen, N3. The assay here is a balance and a spectroscope rather than a crucible: densities to four decimal places, a ratio of specific heats that showed the gas was monatomic, wavelengths matched to the sun. Priority was guarded by sealed notes and telegrams, and disputes are given here as positions with their evidence. Some voices are missing. Ramsay's letters to his wife Margaret, often quoted in later biographies, were not available for this chapter, and the laboratory assistants, glassblowers and liquid-air workers left no accounts of their own that were found.

intro: In mid-August 1896 a Tagish family party at the mouth of the Klondike River went up a side stream called Rabbit Creek and found gold lying thick in the gravel. The party was Keish (Skookum Jim), his nephew Káa Goox (Dawson Charlie), his sister Shaaw Tláa (Kate Carmack) and her American husband George Carmack. On 17 August the men staked the creek, soon renamed Bonanza, and Carmack's name went on the Discovery claim. Within weeks the miners of Forty Mile and the older creeks had staked everything in reach. Who found the gold is still disputed, and this chapter treats it as positions with evidence. Carmack later claimed the find. The surveyor William Ogilvie, who interviewed every party, credited Keish with the find on Bonanza and gave the Nova Scotian Robert Henderson, who had sent Carmack into the area but did not want his Tagish companions there, the title of discoverer of the Klondike. Indigenous oral histories credit Shaaw Tláa with the first large nugget. A guidebook of 1897 named only Henderson, and gave a different date. The camp at the Klondike mouth already belonged to someone. Tr'ochëk was the salmon fishery of the Hän-speaking Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in under Chief Isaac. Their own heritage account says they were forced out within a month of the strike. Over the winter of 1897–98 they moved to Moosehide, three miles downriver, while the town of Dawson spread over the flat beside them. No firsthand account by Chief Isaac from 1896–99 was found. His later words survive as reporters printed them, and his people's memory survives in their own published histories. Both are placed here beside the police reports. News reached the outside world only in July 1897. The Excelsior docked at San Francisco on 14 July and the Portland at Seattle on 17 July, and the Post-Intelligencer's story of more than a ton of gold set off a stampede in the middle of a depression. Perhaps a hundred thousand people set out and something over thirty thousand passed down the Yukon. They went over the Chilkoot and White Passes, where Superintendent Sam Steele's North-West Mounted Police raised the flag in February 1898 and turned back anyone without a year's food. They built boats at Lakes Lindeman and Bennett and ran the rapids at Miles Canyon. On Palm Sunday, 3 April 1898, avalanches below the Chilkoot summit killed more than sixty people. Ottawa made the Yukon a separate territory on 13 June 1898. Dawson's population peaked that summer (estimates range from under 20,000 to 30,000 or more), and in 1899 the beach gold of Nome began to draw it away. Most of the record is not diaries. It is a police report, a surveyor's memoir, newspaper extras, a promoter's guidebook, a typed diary kept by one of Jack London's partners, Steele's pocket diary and memoir, and two later memoirs told by a Tagish nephew and a Chicago woman who crossed the pass pregnant. title: The Great Star: The Cullinan Diamond from Pit to Sceptre
eyes: African mineworkers at the Premier mine (collective)
Frederick Henry Hatch (with George Steuart Corstorphine)
William Waldegrave Palmer, 2nd Earl of Selborne
Edward VII and the Royal Household

places: Geological Society of South Africa, Johannesburg
Johannesburg and Pretoria; the mine at Elandsfontein
Letter from Barbon Manor, Kirkby Lonsdale, to Churchill
Masterton, Wellington and other New Zealand towns
Premier mine and its compounds; homes across southern and central Africa

intro: Late on a January afternoon in 1905, on his round of the Premier mine's open pit near Pretoria, the surface manager Frederick Wells saw something bright in the wall and cut it out with a pocket-knife. It was a diamond of about 3,106 metric carats, more than three times the size of any found before. It took the name of the company chairman, Thomas Cullinan. Within three years it had been bought by the colony, given to the King, split in Amsterdam, and set in the regalia of the British Crown. Almost none of the record is diaries. This chapter is built from what does survive: company papers and later family recollections, the Johannesburg press, the geologists' printed description, the printed debates of the Transvaal Legislative Assembly, the private letters of politicians and the Governor (known through Bill Guest's archival study), Colonial Office telegrams, the press cables that carried the story across the Empire, the Asscher firm's photographs, and the Royal Collection's records of where the stones were set. Forms are tagged honestly; legends are marked as legends. The stone's politics are the heart of the matter. In August 1907, five years after the end of the South African War, Louis Botha's Het Volk government asked the depressed colony to pay £150,000 for it as a birthday gift to Edward VII. Afrikaner generals spoke for it, one of them admitting he could not yet call himself loyal. Labour voted with the government. The English-speaking Progressives voted against, in public on grounds of hardship and in private calling it a bribe. The vote was 42 to 19. The men who dug the stone are the hardest to see. The Premier pit was worked by Black African labourers, among them several hundred men recruited from Nyasaland in 1906. Recruiting there was stopped because so many died. No firsthand account by any of them has been found, and the worker who in some accounts first saw the stone is not named in any source consulted. The chapter gives them an eye of their own, built from the official records that counted them. The coda follows the stones into the Sceptre and the Imperial State Crown in 1909–10. It ends with the calls since 2022 for their return to South Africa. Those calls, and the answer that the stone was bought and given by an elected colonial government, are set out as positions.
